note.text: A conditional links a condition and a result. Common zero-condition models use present forms for general patterns. A first-condition model uses if + present and will + base for a possible future. A second-condition model commonly uses if + past and would + base for an imagined present or future. A third-condition model uses if + past perfect and would have + participle for an unreal past. These are useful patterns, not a claim that every possible conditional must fit one rigid template.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to select and justify a conditional model for a general, possible, imagined or unreal-past relationship. Builds on: tense revision and reported viewpoints. Leads to: accurate qualifications in explanatory writing.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern
sections.text: A conditional links a condition and a result. Common zero-condition models use present forms for general patterns. A first-condition model uses if + present and will + base for a possible future. A second-condition model commonly uses if + past and would + base for an imagined present or future. A third-condition model uses if + past perfect and would have + participle for an unreal past. These are useful patterns, not a claim that every possible conditional must fit one rigid template.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original models: If the room is available, the club meets there as a general rule. If it is available tomorrow, we will meet there. If we had another room, we would share the work. If we had booked earlier, we would have obtained the room. The last situation is imagined about the past; it does not report that the earlier booking actually happened.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Choose the intended time and degree of reality before the form. In the ordinary first-condition model, do not insert will into the if-clause simply because the time is future. Other modal uses exist, so a special context can justify another construction. Clause order can change without reversing the condition and result.

If the room is free tomorrow, we will meet there.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: Every conditional necessarily concerns one future event. Correction: A zero-condition model can describe a general pattern.
The ordinary first-condition model always requires will in both clauses. Correction: Use present in the if-clause and will plus base in the result here.
The past form here proves the imagined room existed yesterday. Correction: The past form can mark hypothetical distance rather than past time.
The third-condition model reports that the earlier condition actually happened. Correction: The model imagines a past alternative, rather than asserting its occurrence.

pick.r: If Bih arrives early, she will help.
w: If Bih will arrives early, she will help.
If Bih arrive early, she will helped.
If Bih arrived yesterday, she will helped yesterday.
e: The ordinary if-clause uses present, with correct agreement.
Arrives and help are required in this pattern.
This mixes incompatible time and verb patterns.
pick.y: If-present links to will plus base.

pick.r: If Ayuk had more time, he would read.
w: If Ayuk had more time, he would reads.
If Ayuk has more time, he would to read.
If Ayuk had more time, he will reading.
e: Use base read after would.
Would does not take to in this pattern.
Will reading does not form the requested model.
pick.y: If-past plus would-base fits the stated imagined situation.

pick.r: If Bih had left earlier, she would have arrived on time.
w: If Bih had leave earlier, she would have arrived on time.
If Bih had left earlier, she would have arrive on time.
If Bih had left earlier, she would has arrived on time.
e: Had takes the participle left.
Have takes the participle arrived.
Would is followed by base have.
pick.y: Both perfect patterns need the appropriate participles.

pick.q: Which reformulation preserves the conditional relationship?
pick.r: We will meet if the room is free.
w: The room is free if we will meet, with the same asserted condition.
We will meet although the room is free, with identical meaning.
The room was free because we met, with identical meaning.
e: That changes the condition’s direction and form.
Although expresses concession, not the same condition.
That invents past time and a causal relationship.
pick.y: Moving the if-clause does not reverse which event is the condition.
